children.title: Classical Hessian Models
children.top_down_role: Twice-smooth specialization and its local curvature representation.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is twice Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local second-order model is the quadratic form \(w\mapsto\langle w,\nabla^2f(\bar x)w\rangle\).

notation.meaning: gradient of f at the reference point
Hessian of f at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional twice-smooth Taylor model with the standard one-half normalization.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\), twice Fréchet differentiability gives
\[
f(\bar x+t w)=f(\bar x)+t\langle\nabla f(\bar x),w\rangle+\tfrac12t^2\langle w,\nabla^2f(\bar x)w\rangle+o(t^2)
\]
as \(t\to0\). Consequently,
\[
\lim_{t\to0}\frac{2\bigl(f(\bar x+t w)-f(\bar x)-t\langle\nabla f(\bar x),w\rangle\bigr)}{t^2}=\langle w,\nabla^2f(\bar x)w\rangle.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice-smooth function, the Hessian quadratic form is exactly the second-order term in the local Taylor expansion.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Laplace–Beltrami and tangential Hessian representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the principal second-order surface operators and states their canonical-extension and curvature identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(\Omega\) is of class \(C^3\) and let \(f\in C^2(\Gamma)\). Define
\[
\Delta_\Gamma f:=\operatorname{div}_\Gamma(\nabla_\Gamma f),
\qquad D_\Gamma^2f:=D_\Gamma(\nabla_\Gamma f).
\]
Then
\[
\Delta_\Gamma f=\left.\Delta(f\circ p)\right|_\Gamma.
\]
The tangential Hessian need not be symmetric and satisfies
\[
D_\Gamma^2f-(D^2b\,\nabla_\Gamma f)n^*
=\left.D^2(f\circ p)\right|_\Gamma
=(D_\Gamma^2f)^*-n(D^2b\,\nabla_\Gamma f)^*.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
D_\Gamma^2f+(D_\Gamma^2f)^*(nn^*)
=\left.D^2(f\circ p)\right|_\Gamma
=(D_\Gamma^2f)^*+(nn^*)D_\Gamma^2f,
\]
so
\[
P D_\Gamma^2f=(P D_\Gamma^2f)^*.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a C2 function on the boundary of a C3 domain, the Laplace–Beltrami operator is the tangential divergence of the tangential gradient and equals the boundary restriction of the ambient Laplacian of the nearest-point extension. The tangential Hessian is generally nonsymmetric; its discrepancy from the canonical-extension Hessian is determined by curvature and the first tangential derivative, while its tangentially projected part is symmetric.
assumptions_latex: p\text{ is the nearest-point projection and }b\text{ is the signed-distance function}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta_\Gamma f=\left.\Delta(f\circ p)\right|_\Gamma,\quad D_\Gamma^2f-(D^2b\nabla_\Gamma f)n^*=\left.D^2(f\circ p)\right|_\Gamma,\quad PD_\Gamma^2f=(PD_\Gamma^2f)^*

children.top_down_role: Directional second-order models beyond twice-smooth functions.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and the directional derivative \(df(\bar x)(w)\) exists finitely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When the displayed limit exists, it defines the second-order directional derivative \(d^2f(\bar x)(w)\).

notation.meaning: second-order directional derivative in direction w

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided second-order directional derivative along a fixed ray.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The second-order directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) is
\[
d^2f(\bar x)(w):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+t w)-f(\bar x)-t\,df(\bar x)(w)}{\tfrac12t^2},
\]
provided this extended-real limit exists. The lower second-order directional derivative is obtained by replacing the limit with \(\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\); it remains meaningful when the ordinary limit fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This derivative measures the residual quadratic growth along one fixed direction after subtracting the first-order directional term.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization of twice semidifferentiability for B-differentiable functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent existence, continuity, and second-order expansion conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be B-differentiable at \(\bar x\) in an open set \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). Then \(f\) is twice semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) if and only if: (i) \(f^{(2)}(\bar x;v)\) exists for every \(v\in\mathbb R^n\); (ii) \(f^{(2)}(\bar x;\cdot)\) is continuous on \(\mathbb R^n\); and (iii), for every \(x\) sufficiently near \(\bar x\), \[f(x)=f(\bar x)+f'(\bar x;x-\bar x)+\frac12f^{(2)}(\bar x;x-\bar x)+o(\|x-\bar x\|^2).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a B-differentiable function, twice semidifferentiability is equivalent to existence of every second directional derivative, continuity of the resulting directional function, and a uniform local second-order expansion with a little-o squared remainder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is twice semidifferentiable at }\bar x\iff\left[\begin{array}{l}f^{(2)}(\bar x;v)\text{ exists for all }v\in\mathbb R^n,\\ f^{(2)}(\bar x;\cdot)\text{ is continuous},\\ f(x)=f(\bar x)+f'(\bar x;x-\bar x)+\frac12f^{(2)}(\bar x;x-\bar x)+o(\|x-\bar x\|^2)\end{array}\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order directional derivatives and twice semidifferentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and basic identities for second-order directional and subderivative models of a real-valued semidifferentiable function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\), where \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open, and suppose \(f\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\in\mathcal O\). When the limit exists, define \(\frac12 f^{(2)}(\bar x;v)=\lim_{\tau\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau v)-f(\bar x)-\tau f'(\bar x;v)}{\tau^2}\). For \(v,w\in\mathbb R^n\), define \(\frac12\mathrm d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w)=\liminf_{w'\to w,\,\tau\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w')-f(\bar x)-\tau v^\top w'}{\tau^2}\), and define \(\frac12\mathrm d^2f(\bar x)(w)=\liminf_{w'\to w,\,\tau\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w')-f(\bar x)-\tau\mathrm df(\bar x)(w')}{\tau^2}\). The functions \(f^{(2)}(\bar x;\cdot)\) and \(\mathrm d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(\cdot)\) are positively homogeneous of degree two. The function is twice directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\) when it is directionally differentiable there and \(f^{(2)}(\bar x;v)\) exists for every \(v\). It is twice semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) when it is semidifferentiable there and the defining limit for \(\mathrm d^2f(\bar x)(w)\) exists for every \(w\). In the latter case, \(\mathrm d^2f(\bar x)(w)=f^{(2)}(\bar x;w)\) for every \(w\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order directional derivative removes the first directional term from a directional difference quotient. The second-order subderivatives use lower limits under simultaneous perturbation of the direction. These objects are positively homogeneous of degree two. Twice directional differentiability requires all fixed-direction limits, whereas twice semidifferentiability requires the perturbed-direction limits. Under twice semidifferentiability, the unparameterized second-order subderivative equals the second-order directional derivative in every direction.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R\text{ is semidifferentiable at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is twice semidifferentiable at }\bar x\implies \mathrm d^2f(\bar x)(w)=f^{(2)}(\bar x;w)\quad\forall w\in\mathbb R^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order semidifferentiable chain rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition rule for a twice semidifferentiable inner mapping and a Fréchet-differentiable, twice semidifferentiable outer function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be twice semidifferentiable near \(\bar x\), and let \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) be Fréchet differentiable and twice semidifferentiable at \(\Phi(\bar x)\). Then \(f=g\circ\Phi\) is twice semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\), and for every \(w\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\mathrm d^2f(\bar x)(w)=g'\!\left(\Phi(\bar x);\mathrm d^2\Phi(\bar x)(w)\right)+\mathrm d^2g\!\left(\Phi(\bar x)\right)\!\left(\Phi'(\bar x;w)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite is twice semidifferentiable when the inner mapping is twice semidifferentiable nearby and the outer function is both Fréchet differentiable and twice semidifferentiable at the image point. Its second-order derivative is the outer first derivative applied to the inner second derivative plus the outer second derivative evaluated along the inner first derivative.
assumptions_latex: \Phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ is twice semidifferentiable near }\bar x
g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\text{ is Fréchet differentiable at }\Phi(\bar x)
g\text{ is twice semidifferentiable at }\Phi(\bar x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is twice semidifferentiable at }\bar x\text{ and }\mathrm d^2f(\bar x)(w)=g'(\Phi(\bar x);\mathrm d^2\Phi(\bar x)(w))+\mathrm d^2g(\Phi(\bar x))(\Phi'(\bar x;w))\quad\forall w\in\mathbb R^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity of the second derivative under twice semidifferentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality and continuity of directional second-order models under twice semidifferentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is twice semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) in an open set \(\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), then \(\mathrm d^2f(\bar x)(\cdot)=f^{(2)}(\bar x;\cdot)\), and this common function is continuous on \(\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order chain rule with a piecewise-affine inner mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplified second-order composition rule when the inner mapping is piecewise affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be piecewise affine, let \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), and suppose \(g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) is twice semidifferentiable at \(\Phi(\bar x)\). Then \(f=g\circ\Phi\) is twice semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\), and for every \(w\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\mathrm d^2f(\bar x)(w)=\mathrm d^2g\!\left(\Phi(\bar x)\right)\!\left(\Phi'(\bar x;w)\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a twice semidifferentiable outer function with a piecewise-affine inner mapping preserves twice semidifferentiability. Because the inner mapping has no second-order contribution, the composite second derivative is the outer second derivative evaluated along the inner directional derivative.
assumptions_latex: g:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\text{ is twice semidifferentiable at }\Phi(\bar x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is twice semidifferentiable at }\bar x\text{ and }\mathrm d^2f(\bar x)(w)=\mathrm d^2g(\Phi(\bar x))(\Phi'(\bar x;w))\quad\forall w\in\mathbb R^n.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-dimensional second-subderivative definition with one-half normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar–Wets lower epigraphical second-order quotient convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), set
\[
\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+t w)-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2}.
\]
The second subderivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\bar v\) is
\[
d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w').
\]
The perturbation \(w'\to w\) distinguishes this lower epigraphical object from a fixed-ray second-order directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second subderivative is the lower epigraphical limit of quadratic difference quotients after subtracting a specified covector’s linear term.
knowledge_statements.title: Second Subderivatives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a standard second-subderivative convention, but no inspectable source establishes the normalization and joint liminf convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Twice semidifferentiable and twice epi-differentiable functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order regularity defined by continuous convergence or epi-convergence of difference quotients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} and f(\bar x)<\infty. The function f is twice semidifferentiable at \bar x if it is semidifferentiable there and
\[
\Delta_\tau^2f(\bar x)\to d^2f(\bar x)\quad\text{continuously as }\tau\searrow0.
\]
Equivalently, for every w, the joint limit as \tau\searrow0 and w'\to w of
\[
\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w')-f(\bar x)-\tau df(\bar x)(w')}{\tfrac12\tau^2}
\]
exists and equals d^2f(\bar x)(w).

The function f is twice epi-differentiable at \bar x for v if
\[
\Delta_\tau^2f(\bar x\mid v)\xrightarrow{e}d^2f(\bar x\mid v)\quad\text{as }\tau\searrow0,
\]
and is properly twice epi-differentiable if this limit is proper. Equivalently, for every w and every sequence \tau^\nu\searrow0, there are w^\nu\to w such that
\[
\frac{f(\bar x+\tau^\nu w^\nu)-f(\bar x)-\tau^\nu\langle v,w^\nu\rangle}{\tfrac12(\tau^\nu)^2}\to d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w).
\]
Twice epi-differentiability does not require first-order epi-differentiability, but for every w\in\operatorname{dom}d^2f(\bar x\mid v) it implies existence of the first-order epi-derivative in direction w.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twice semidifferentiability requires first-order semidifferentiability and continuous convergence of the ordinary second-order quotients. Twice epi-differentiability requires epigraphical convergence of the covector-relative quotients; it is proper when the resulting second subderivative is proper. It does not assume global first-order epi-differentiability, although it yields the directional first-order epi-derivative on the domain of the second subderivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ twice semidifferentiable at }\bar x\iff f\text{ is semidifferentiable at }\bar x\text{ and }\Delta_\tau^2f(\bar x)\to d^2f(\bar x)\text{ continuously};\quad f\text{ twice epi-differentiable at }\bar x\text{ for }v\iff\Delta_\tau^2f(\bar x\mid v)\xrightarrow{e}d^2f(\bar x\mid v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive homogeneity of degree p
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real positive homogeneity, including the permitted value at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For p>0, a function h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} is positively homogeneous of degree p if
\[
h(\lambda w)=\lambda^p h(w)\quad\text{for every }\lambda>0\text{ and }w\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\]
and h(0)<+\infty. Necessarily h(0)\in\{0,-\infty\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is positively homogeneous of degree p greater than zero when scaling its argument by every positive scalar scales its value by that scalar to the p-th power, and its value at zero is below positive infinity. Its value at zero must then be zero or negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[(\forall\lambda>0)(\forall w)\ h(\lambda w)=\lambda^p h(w)\ \land\ h(0)<+\infty\bigr],\qquad h(0)\in\{0,-\infty\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural and domain properties of second subderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower semicontinuity, quadratic homogeneity, covector dependence, and properness restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} with f(\bar x)<\infty. The functions d^2f(\bar x) and d^2f(\bar x\mid v) are lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous of degree 2, and d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w) is concave as a function of v. Moreover,
\[
d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w)=+\infty\ \text{if }\langle v,w\rangle<df(\bar x)(w),\qquad d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w)=-\infty\ \text{if }\langle v,w\rangle>df(\bar x)(w).
\]
Hence finiteness requires \langle v,w\rangle=df(\bar x)(w), and
\[
\operatorname{dom}d^2f(\bar x\mid v)\subset\{w:df(\bar x)(w)\leq\langle v,w\rangle\}.
\]
If d^2f(\bar x\mid v) is proper, then
\[
v\in\widehat\partial f(\bar x),\qquad \operatorname{dom}d^2f(\bar x\mid v)\subset\{w:df(\bar x)(w)=\langle v,w\rangle\}\subset N_{\widehat\partial f(\bar x)}(v).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second subderivatives are lower semicontinuous and homogeneous of degree two, and the covector-relative value is concave in the covector. A strict mismatch between the directional derivative and the covector pairing forces positive or negative infinity. Properness therefore requires a regular subgradient covector and confines the effective domain to equality directions, which lie in the normal cone to the regular subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d^2f(\bar x),d^2f(\bar x\mid v)\text{ are lsc and degree-2 positively homogeneous};\quad d^2f(\bar x\mid v)\text{ proper}\Rightarrow v\in\widehat\partial f(\bar x),\ \operatorname{dom}d^2f(\bar x\mid v)\subset\{df(\bar x)=\langle v,\cdot\rangle\}\subset N_{\widehat\partial f(\bar x)}(v).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The second epi-derivative, when defined, is the epigraphical limit of \(\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\).

notation.meaning: quadratic difference quotient relative to the covector

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard sequential definition of a second epi-derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential finite-dimensional epigraphical limit as the scale tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(q_t:=\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) for \(t>0\). A function \(q:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is the second epi-derivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\bar v\) when
\[
q=\operatorname*{e-lim}_{t\downarrow0}q_t.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(w\), every sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(w_k\to w\) satisfy \(q(w)\le\liminf_k q_{t_k}(w_k)\), and for every sequence \(t_k\downarrow0\) there exist \(w_k\to w\) with \(q(w)\ge\limsup_k q_{t_k}(w_k)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Strong Second-Order Majorant Yields a Dual Minorant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers a quadratically coercive second-order upper model to a lower model of the Fenchel conjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f\in\operatorname{Conv}^{2}(\mathbb R^n), x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f, s\in\partial f(x_0), and let \varphi_s be directionally quadratic. Assume that for some c>0, \varphi_s(h)\ge	frac c2\|h\|^2 for every h\in\mathbb R^n, and that
\[f(x_0+h)\le f(x_0)+\langle s,hangle+\varphi_s(h)+o(\|h\|^2).\]
Then \varphi_s^* defines a second-order minorization of f^* at s associated with x_0; equivalently,
\[f^*(s+p)\ge f^*(s)+\langle x_0,pangle+\varphi_s^*(p)+o(\|p\|^2).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformly quadratic second-order upper model of a convex function becomes a lower second-order model of its Fenchel conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \varphi_s\text{ defines a second-order majorization of }f\text{ at }x_0\text{ associated with }s
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^*(s+p)\ge f^*(s)+\langle x_0,p\rangle+\varphi_s^*(p)+o(\|p\|^2).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional second-order regularity of an extended-real-valued function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical definition, its finiteness boundary, and the convex-continuous directional reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R} be finite at y_0. The function g is outer second-order regular (respectively, second-order regular) at y_0 in direction d if g_-^{\downarrow}(y_0,d) is finite and \operatorname{epi}g is outer second-order regular (respectively, second-order regular) at (y_0,g(y_0)) in direction (d,g_-^{\downarrow}(y_0,d)). It is regular at y_0 without a specified direction when \operatorname{epi}g has the corresponding regularity at (y_0,g(y_0)). If g is convex and continuous at y_0, then g_-^{\downarrow}(y_0,d)=g'(y_0;d) is finite for every d; moreover, for \gamma>g'(y_0;d), T^2_{\operatorname{epi}g}((y_0,g(y_0)),(d,\gamma))=Y\times\mathbb R, so regularity need only be checked in directions (d,g'(y_0;d)).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional second-order regularity of a function is defined through second-order regularity of its epigraph in the direction formed from the base direction and the finite lower directional epiderivative. Infinite epiderivatives do not define such a direction. For a convex function continuous at the base point, all directional derivatives are finite and only boundary directions with vertical component equal to the directional derivative require verification.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the reduction statement, }g\text{ is convex and continuous at }y_0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is (outer) second-order regular at }y_0\text{ in direction }d\iff\operatorname{epi}g\text{ is correspondingly regular at }(y_0,g(y_0))\text{ in direction }(d,g_-^{\downarrow}(y_0,d));\ \text{in the convex-continuous case only }(d,g'(y_0;d))\text{ need be checked}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order epiderivative criterion for outer regularity of a convex sublevel set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The pathwise inequality is sufficient under lower semicontinuity, convexity, and Slater's condition, and becomes necessary when the function is continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R} be lower semicontinuous and convex, let K:=\{y\in Y:g(y)\leq0\}, and suppose that g(\bar y)<0 for some \bar y\in Y. Let g(y_0)=0 and g_-^{\downarrow}(y_0,d)=0. If every path y(t)=y_0+td+\tfrac12t^2r(t)\in K, t\geq0, satisfying tr(t)\to0 as t\downarrow0 also satisfies \limsup_{t\downarrow0}g_-^{\downarrow\downarrow}(y_0;d,r(t))\leq0, then K is outer second-order regular at y_0 in direction d. If g is continuous, the converse also holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-semicontinuous convex inequality satisfying Slater's condition, the stated second-order epiderivative inequality along every feasible second-order path implies directional outer second-order regularity of the boundary sublevel set. When the function is continuous, outer second-order regularity also implies that pathwise inequality.
assumptions_latex: g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall y(t)=y_0+td+\tfrac12t^2r(t)\in K\text{ with }tr(t)\to0,\ \limsup_{t\downarrow0}g_-^{\downarrow\downarrow}(y_0;d,r(t))\leq0\right]\Rightarrow K\text{ is outer second-order regular at }y_0\text{ in direction }d;\quad g\text{ continuous}\Rightarrow\text{the converse implication}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper twice epi-differentiability relative to a fixed first-order covector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if the family \(\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) epi-converges as \(t\downarrow0\) to a proper extended-real function. In that case,
\[
\operatorname*{e-lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)=d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v),
\]
where the equality follows because the epigraphical lower limit is the second subderivative. Properness excludes a limit identically equal to \(+\infty\) or taking the value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twice epi-differentiability means that quadratic difference quotients epi-converge to a proper second-order model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure of second subderivatives of convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the additional consequences available under twice epi-differentiability and the characterization of twice semidifferentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be proper and convex, let \bar{x}\in\operatorname{dom}f, and let \bar{v}\in\partial f(\bar{x}). Then d^2f(\bar{x}\mid\bar{v})\ge 0 everywhere and d^2f(\bar{x}\mid\bar{v})=\gamma_C^2 for the gauge of a unique closed set C\ni0. If f is twice epi-differentiable at \bar{x} for \bar{v}, then d^2f(\bar{x}\mid\bar{v}) and C are convex. Moreover, f is twice semidifferentiable at \bar{x} for \bar{v} if and only if it is twice epi-differentiable there and d^2f(\bar{x}\mid\bar{v})(w)<\infty for every w; in that case f is differentiable at \bar{x} and \bar{v}=\nabla f(\bar{x}).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function and a subgradient at a domain point, the second subderivative is nonnegative and is the square of the gauge of a unique closed set containing zero. Twice epi-differentiability makes the second subderivative and generating set convex. Twice semidifferentiability is equivalent to twice epi-differentiability plus finiteness in every direction, and it forces differentiability at the base point with the given subgradient equal to the gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d^2f(\bar{x}\mid\bar{v})\ge0,\quad d^2f(\bar{x}\mid\bar{v})=\gamma_C^2\text{ for a unique closed }C\ni0,\quad f\text{ is twice semidifferentiable}\iff f\text{ is twice epi-differentiable and }d^2f(\bar{x}\mid\bar{v})\text{ is finite everywhere}.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The value \(d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)\) measures second-order growth along arcs with velocity \(w\) and acceleration \(z\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard lower parabolic difference-quotient definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower parabolic derivative using velocity and acceleration variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a direction \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and a second-order correction \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the parabolic subderivative is
\[
d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\z'\to z}}\frac{f(\bar x+t w+\tfrac12t^2z')-f(\bar x)-t\,df(\bar x)(w)}{\tfrac12t^2}.
\]
It is an extended-real function of \(z\) for each fixed first-order direction \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The parabolic subderivative records quadratic growth along perturbed arcs having prescribed first-order velocity and second-order acceleration.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parabolic Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional parabolic regularity at a feasible point relative to a compatible covector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be feasible, \(h\in X\), and \(\alpha\in X^*\) satisfy \(\langle\alpha,h\rangle=f_-^{\downarrow}(x,h)\). The function \(f\) is parabolically regular at \(x\) in direction \(h\) for \(\alpha\) if
\[
\inf_{w\in X}\left\{f_-^{\downarrow\downarrow}(x;h,w)-\langle\alpha,w\rangle\right\}=d^2f(x\mid\alpha)(h).
\]
If \(\phi(w):=f_-^{\downarrow\downarrow}(x;h,w)\), this equality is equivalently
\[
d^2f(x\mid\alpha)(h)=-\phi^*(\alpha).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parabolic regularity holds when the general comparison between the covector-adjusted parabolic second-order derivative and the second subderivative is attained as equality. Equivalently, the second subderivative equals the negative conjugate value of the parabolic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{w\in X}\{f_-^{\downarrow\downarrow}(x;h,w)-\langle\alpha,w\rangle\}=d^2f(x\mid\alpha)(h)=-\phi^*(\alpha)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower semicontinuity and comparison inequality for parabolic subderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates the primal parabolic subderivative to the second subderivative relative to a supporting vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}, f(\bar x)<\infty, and df(\bar x)(w)<\infty. Then \(z\mapsto d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)\) is lower semicontinuous. If \(df(\bar x)(w)=\langle v,w\rangle\), then
\[
\inf_z\{d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)-\langle v,z\rangle\}\ge d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w).
\]
Moreover, the left-hand side equals the lower limit of \(\Delta_\tau^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w')\) over \(\tau\searrow0\), \(w'\to w\), subject to \((w'-w)/\tau\) being bounded, whereas the right-hand side is the corresponding lower limit without that boundedness restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The parabolic subderivative is lower semicontinuous in its second-order direction. After subtracting the linear term induced by a vector v supporting the first subderivative along w, its infimum bounds the relative second subderivative from below. The infimum corresponds precisely to recovery sequences whose displacement from w is of order τ; dropping this bounded-rate restriction yields the possibly smaller relative second subderivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\mapsto d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)\text{ is lsc},\qquad \inf_z\{d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)-\langle v,z\rangle\}\ge d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parabolic calculus for fully amenable functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes epi-differentiability, regularity, conjugacy, and a composite formula for parabolic subderivatives of fully amenable functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be fully amenable at \(\bar x\). Then \(f\) is parabolically epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for every \(w\in\operatorname{dom}df(\bar x)\) and parabolically regular there for every \(v\in\partial f(\bar x)\). For each such \(w\), \(z\mapsto d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and piecewise linear, and is conjugate to
\[
v\mapsto\begin{cases}-d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w),&v\in\partial f(\bar x\mid w),\\+\infty,&v\notin\partial f(\bar x\mid w),\end{cases}
\quad
\partial f(\bar x\mid w):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in\partial f(\bar x)}\langle v,w\rangle.
\]
If locally \(f=g\circ F\), with \(g\) piecewise linear-quadratic as in full amenability, then
\[
d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)=d^2g(F(\bar x))\bigl(\nabla F(\bar x)w\mid\nabla^2F(\bar x)[w,w]+\nabla F(\bar x)z\bigr)
\]
\[
=d^2g(F(\bar x))(\nabla F(\bar x)w)+\max_{y\in Y(\bar x\mid w)}\left\langle y,\nabla^2F(\bar x)[w,w]+\nabla F(\bar x)z\right\rangle,
\]
where \(Y(\bar x\mid w)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in\partial g(F(\bar x))}\langle y,\nabla F(\bar x)w\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full amenability guarantees parabolic epi-differentiability in every direction where the first subderivative is finite and parabolic regularity for every subgradient. The resulting parabolic subderivative is a proper lower-semicontinuous convex piecewise-linear function of the second-order direction, has the stated conjugate description over directionally active subgradients, and obeys an explicit composition formula for a smooth mapping followed by a piecewise linear-quadratic function.
assumptions_latex: f=g\circ F\text{ locally, with }g\text{ piecewise linear-quadratic, for the composition formula}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is parabolically epi-differentiable for all }w\in\operatorname{dom}df(\bar x)\text{ and parabolically regular for all }v\in\partial f(\bar x),\text{ with the stated conjugacy and chain formula.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parabolic Regularity and Second Subderivative of a Convex Composite
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A Banach-space composite rule under outer second-order regularity and Robinson constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be Banach spaces, \(F:X\to Y\) be twice continuously differentiable, and \(g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be lower semicontinuous and convex, with \(g(y_0)<+\infty\) for \(y_0:=F(x_0)\). Let \(\gamma\in\partial g(y_0)\) satisfy
\[
\langle\gamma,DF(x_0)h\rangle=g_-^{\downarrow}(y_0,DF(x_0)h).
\]
Set \(d:=DF(x_0)h\) and \(\alpha:=DF(x_0)^*\gamma\). If \(g\) is outer second-order regular at \(y_0\) in direction \(d\) and Robinson's constraint qualification holds, then \(f:=g\circ F\) is parabolically regular at \(x_0\) in direction \(h\) for \(\alpha\), and
\[
d^2f(x_0\mid\alpha)(h)=\inf_{w\in X}\left\{g_-^{\downarrow\downarrow}\!\left(y_0;d,DF(x_0)w+D^2F(x_0)(h,h)\right)-\langle\alpha,w\rangle\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable mapping followed by a lower-semicontinuous convex function, compatibility of a subgradient with the chosen direction, outer second-order regularity of the outer function, and Robinson qualification imply parabolic regularity of the composite and yield the displayed second-subderivative formula.
assumptions_latex: F:X\to Y\text{ is twice continuously differentiable}
g:Y\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex}
g\text{ is outer second-order regular at }y_0\text{ in direction }d
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f=g\circ F\text{ is parabolically regular at }x_0\text{ in direction }h\text{ for }\alpha,\quad d^2f(x_0\mid\alpha)(h)=\inf_{w\in X}\{g_-^{\downarrow\downarrow}(y_0;d,DF(x_0)w+D^2F(x_0)(h,h))-\langle\alpha,w\rangle\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parabolic subderivative and parabolic epi-differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the second-order parabolic growth model and its epigraphical exactness along a first-order direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}, let f(\bar x)<\infty, and suppose df(\bar x)(w)<\infty. For z\in\mathbb{R}^n, the parabolic subderivative is
\[
d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z):=\liminf_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\z'\to z}}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w+\tfrac12\tau^2z')-f(\bar x)-\tau df(\bar x)(w)}{\tfrac12\tau^2},
\]
equivalently \(d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid\cdot)=\operatorname{e-liminf}_{\tau\searrow0}\Delta_\tau^2f(\bar x)(w\mid\cdot)\). The function is parabolically epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(w\) when this epigraphical lower limit is the proper epigraphical limit. Equivalently, for every \(z\) there are \(z_\tau\to z\) attaining the limiting value, or an arc \(\xi\) with \(\xi(0)=\bar x\), \(\xi'_+(0)=w\), and \(\xi''_+(0)=z\) such that \((f\circ\xi)''_+(0)=d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite-valued base point and a direction with finite first subderivative, the parabolic subderivative is the lower limit of normalized second-order differences along perturbations x̄+τw+(τ²/2)z′. Parabolic epi-differentiability means that these quotients epigraphically converge to a function not identically positive infinity; equivalently, each second-order direction can be realized by convergent perturbations or by a twice right-differentiable arc attaining the parabolic subderivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)=\liminf_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\z'\to z}}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w+\tfrac12\tau^2z')-f(\bar x)-\tau df(\bar x)(w)}{\tfrac12\tau^2}

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parabolic regularity identifies the covector-relative second subderivative with the optimized acceleration model.

notation.meaning: second subderivative relative to the covector

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-form parabolic regularity on directions critical for the chosen covector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is parabolically regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) in the value-form sense if, for every \(w\) with \(df(\bar x)(w)=\langle\bar v,w\rangle\),
\[
d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl\{d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)-\langle\bar v,z\rangle\bigr\},
\]
with the convention that the infimum is \(+\infty\) when every term is \(+\infty\). This condition makes the epigraphical second-order model recoverable from parabolic accelerations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parabolic regularity says the second subderivative equals the best parabolic acceleration model after subtracting the covector pairing.
knowledge_statements.title: Parabolic Regularity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed value identity may be a consequence of a sequence-based parabolic-regularity condition rather than its definition. Exact hypotheses and the intended variant require a source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parabolic regularity of a function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exactness of the comparison between parabolic and relative second subderivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is parabolically regular at \(\bar x\) for \(v\) if \(f(\bar x)<\infty\) and, for every \(w\) satisfying \(df(\bar x)(w)=\langle v,w\rangle\),
\[
\inf_z\{d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)-\langle v,z\rangle\}=d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w).
\]
Equivalently, whenever such a \(w\) also satisfies \(d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w)<\infty\), there are \(\tau^\nu\searrow0\) and \(w^\nu\to w\) such that
\[
\Delta_{\tau^\nu}^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w^\nu)\to d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w),\qquad \limsup_\nu\frac{\lVert w^\nu-w\rVert}{\tau^\nu}<\infty.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parabolic regularity at x̄ for v means that the general comparison inequality between the parabolic and relative second subderivatives is exact for every direction supported by v. Equivalently, every finite relative second-subderivative value in such a direction admits a recovery sequence approaching that direction at a rate bounded by a constant times τ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_z\{d^2f(\bar x)(w\mid z)-\langle v,z\rangle\}=d^2f(\bar x\mid v)(w)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical cone for box-constrained controls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise sign characterization of critical directions relative to the set \(A_0(\bar u)\) and lower and upper control bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a box-feasible control \(\bar u\), define \(C_0(\bar u)\) as the set of all \(h\in L^\infty(\Omega)\) satisfying, almost everywhere, \[h(x)=0\ \text{if }x\in A_0(\bar u),\qquad h(x)\ge0\ \text{if }x\notin A_0(\bar u)\text{ and }\bar u(x)=u_a(x),\qquad h(x)\le0\ \text{if }x\notin A_0(\bar u)\text{ and }\bar u(x)=u_b(x).\] On \(\{x\in\Omega:u_a(x)<\bar u(x)<u_b(x)\}\), the direction \(h(x)\) is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The critical cone contains essentially bounded directions that vanish on the designated set A0, point inward at active lower and upper bounds outside A0, and are unrestricted where the control lies strictly between its bounds.
assumptions_latex: A_0(\bar u)\subseteq\Omega\text{ is the designated set used in the definition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_0(\bar u)=\left\{h\in L^\infty(\Omega):\ h=0\text{ on }A_0(\bar u),\ h\ge0\text{ on }\{\bar u=u_a\}\setminus A_0(\bar u),\ h\le0\text{ on }\{\bar u=u_b\}\setminus A_0(\bar u)\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The outer second-order tangent set to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) is
\[
T_C^2(\bar x,w):=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-\bar x-tw}{\tfrac12t^2}.
\]
Equivalently, \(z\in T_C^2(\bar x,w)\) precisely when there exist sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(z_k\to z\) such that
\[
\bar x+t_k w+\tfrac12t_k^2z_k\in C
\]
for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer second-order tangents are acceleration limits realized along at least one sequence of feasible parabolic arcs.

children.title: Parabolic Tangent Geometry

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, \(\bar x\in C\), and \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parabolic derivability is the equality \(T_C^{i,2}(\bar x,w)=T_C^2(\bar x,w)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parabolic derivability along one tangent direction.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196
A. Inner and Outer Limits p. 109

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(C\) is parabolically derivable at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) if
\[
T_C^{i,2}(\bar x,w)=T_C^2(\bar x,w).
\]
Thus every acceleration obtainable along some vanishing sequence is obtainable, up to convergent acceleration perturbations, along every vanishing sequence. If this equality holds for every \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\), then \(C\) is parabolically derivable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parabolic derivability means the inner and outer second-order tangent sets coincide, eliminating dependence on the chosen step-size sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Parabolic Tangent Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Parabolic geometry of fully amenable sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes parabolic derivability, regularity, second-order tangent geometry, and its support-function representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fully amenable set is parabolically derivable in every tangent direction and parabolically regular for every normal vector. Its second-order tangent set in each tangent direction is nonempty and polyhedral, and its support function equals the negative second subderivative of the indicator precisely for normal vectors orthogonal to the direction; otherwise it is positive infinity.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is fully amenable at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_C^2(\bar x\mid w)\ne\varnothing\text{ is polyhedral},\qquad \sigma_{T_C^2(\bar x\mid w)}(v)=\begin{cases}-d^2\delta_C(\bar x\mid v)(w),&v\in N_C(\bar x),\ v\perp w,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Tangent Sets and Parabolic Derivability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines directional second-order tangent geometry and distinguishes sequentially attainable accelerations from full feasible-arc attainability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\bar x\in C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\), define \[T_C^2(\bar x\mid w):=\limsup_{\tau\searrow0}\frac{C-\bar x-\tau w}{\tfrac12\tau^2}.\] The set \(C\) is parabolically derivable at \(\bar x\) for \(w\) when this nonempty outer limit is a full limit; equivalently, every \(z\in T_C^2(\bar x\mid w)\) is realized by an arc \(\xi:[0,\varepsilon]\to C\) satisfying \(\xi(0)=\bar x\), \(\xi'_+(0)=w\), and \(\xi''_+(0)=z\). Without parabolic derivability, some such \(z\) may be attainable only along sequences. The set \(T_C^2(\bar x\mid w)\) need not be a cone and may be empty; for \(C=\{(x_1,x_2):x_1^4-x_2^3=0\}\), \(\bar x=(0,0)\), and \(w=(1,0)\), it is empty and \(C\) is not parabolically derivable in direction \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order tangent set consists of limiting second-order corrections to motion from x-bar in tangent direction w. Parabolic derivability requires every such correction to arise from a feasible arc, not merely from selected sequences. This set may be empty or fail to be a cone; the cusp x1^4=x2^3 at the origin in direction (1,0) gives an empty set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_C^2(\bar x\mid w)=\limsup_{\tau\searrow0}\frac{C-\bar x-\tau w}{\tfrac12\tau^2},\quad C\text{ is parabolically derivable iff the nonempty outer limit is a full limit with the stated arc realization.}

children.title: Primal Curvature Representations
children.top_down_role: Second-order curvature information expressed through feasible-set displacement geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, \(\bar x\in C\), \(\bar v\in N_C(\bar x)\), and \(w\in K_C(\bar x,\bar v)\).
\(C\) is parabolically derivable and parabolically regular at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) relative to \(\bar v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The curvature value is the negative support function \(-\sigma_{T_C^2(\bar x,w)}(\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator-function curvature represented through feasible parabolic accelerations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated derivability and regularity hypotheses, the second subderivative of the indicator function has the primal representation
\[
d^2\delta_C(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=\inf_{z\in T_C^2(\bar x,w)}\{-\langle\bar v,z\rangle\}=-\sigma_{T_C^2(\bar x,w)}(\bar v).
\]
The infimum over the empty set is \(+\infty\). Thus the covector-relative curvature of \(C\) in the critical direction \(w\) is determined by the support of its feasible second-order accelerations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under parabolic regularity, indicator curvature equals the negative support of the second-order tangent set in the normal direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Curvature Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The support-function identity is algebraically consistent, but the exact derivability, regularity, and normal-cone hypotheses under which it represents the indicator's second subderivative require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distortion-coefficient characterization of a Ricci lower bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For an n-dimensional Riemannian manifold equipped with its volume measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\) be an \(n\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold equipped with its volume measure, and let \(K\in\mathbb R\). Then
\[
\operatorname{Ric}\ge K
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\bar\beta_t(x,y)\ge\beta_t^{(K,n)}(x,y)
\]
for all \(x,y\in M\) and \(t\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Riemannian manifold has Ricci curvature bounded below by K exactly when its distortion coefficients dominate the dimension-n reference coefficients for every pair of points and every interpolation time.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ carries its Riemannian volume measure}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Ric}\ge K\Longleftrightarrow\forall x,y\in M\ \forall t\in[0,1],\ \bar\beta_t(x,y)\ge\beta_t^{(K,n)}(x,y).

children.title: Primal–Dual Curvature Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Regimes connecting primal curvature descriptions with dual normal constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(\bar v\in N_C(\bar x)\), and \(\delta_C\) is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DN_C(\bar x,\bar v)(w)=\partial\!\left(\tfrac12 d_e^2\delta_C(\bar x\mid\bar v)\right)(w)\) for every \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex twice-epi-differentiable form of the primal–dual correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the second epi-derivative by
\[
d_e^2\delta_C(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\operatorname*{e\!\!-\!lim}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\delta_C(\bar x+tw)-\delta_C(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2}.
\]
Then the proto-derivative of the normal mapping, which equals its graphical derivative under the stated hypothesis, satisfies
\[
DN_C(\bar x,\bar v)(w)=\partial\!\left(\tfrac12d_e^2\delta_C(\bar x\mid\bar v)\right)(w)
\quad\text{for every }w\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Hence primal second-order epigraphical curvature determines the dual variation of normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex twice-epi-differentiable set indicator, the derivative of the normal mapping equals the subdifferential of one-half its second epi-derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Curvature Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The duality content kind and finite-dimensional convex scope fit the terminal container, and the displayed correspondence is plausible under the stated normalization. However, no citation is supplied, and the precise factor, twice-epi-differentiability hypothesis, proto-derivative conclusion, and equality with the graphical derivative require an authoritative theorem locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The graphical derivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is the positively homogeneous multifunction \(DF(\bar x,\bar y):\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) defined by
\[
DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^m\mid (u,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\) when some \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \((u_k,v_k)\to(u,v)\) satisfy \(\bar y+t_kv_k\in F(\bar x+t_ku_k)\) for every \(k\).

children.title: Strict Graphical Derivatives

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_*F(\bar x,\bar y)(u)=\{v:(u,v)\in T^P_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the paratingent-cone convention for the strict graphical derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The strict graphical derivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is defined through the paratingent cone by
\[
D_*F(\bar x,\bar y)(u):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^m\mid (u,v)\in T^P_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Thus \(v\in D_*F(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\) exactly when there exist graph points \((x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y)\), numbers \(t_k\downarrow0\), and \((u_k,v_k)\to(u,v)\) such that \((x_k+t_ku_k,y_k+t_kv_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) for all \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict graphical derivative permits difference quotients based at arbitrary nearby graph points, capturing uniform local graph variation.

The limiting coderivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is the multifunction \(D^*F(\bar x,\bar y):\mathbb{R}^m\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) given by

D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid (x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivatives of a Continuous Linear Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computes the normal and mixed coderivatives of a continuous linear operator and states its N-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear and continuous. Then, for every \(\bar x\in X\), \(A\) is \(N\)-regular at \(\bar x\), and for every \(y^*\in Y^*\),
\[
D_N^*A(\bar x)(y^*)=D_M^*A(\bar x)(y^*)=\{A^*y^*\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous linear operator is N-regular at every point, and both its normal and mixed coderivatives map each dual vector to the singleton containing its adjoint image.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is proto-differentiable precisely when \(\Delta_tF\) has a graphical limit as \(t\downarrow0\); that limit is \(F'_{\bar x,\bar y}\).

source_refs.locator: 4.4 Sensitivity Analysis for Variational Systems p. 421
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), define the difference-quotient multifunction
\[
\Delta_tF(u):=\frac{F(\bar x+tu)-\bar y}{t}.
\]
The multifunction \(F\) is proto-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) if a multifunction \(F'_{\bar x,\bar y}\) exists such that
\[
\Delta_tF\xrightarrow{g}F'_{\bar x,\bar y}\quad\text{as }t\downarrow0,
\]
where graphical convergence means Painlevé–Kuratowski convergence of the graphs. The limit \(F'_{\bar x,\bar y}\) is the proto-derivative; when it exists, its graph equals \(T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proto-differentiability requires the scaled graph increments of a multifunction to converge graphically to a single derivative multifunction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The limiting second-order subdifferential of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\bar v\) is the multifunction \(\partial^2f(\bar x,\bar v):\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) defined by
\[
\partial^2f(\bar x,\bar v)(u):=D^*(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)(u).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
w\in\partial^2f(\bar x,\bar v)(u)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(w,-u)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}\partial f}(\bar x,\bar v).
\]
For a twice continuously differentiable finite-valued function, this set reduces to \(\{\nabla^2f(\bar x)u\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting second-order subdifferential is the limiting coderivative of the first-order limiting subgradient mapping.

Equivalently,

w\in\breve\partial^{\,2}f(\bar x,\bar v)(u)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(w,-u)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}\partial f}(\bar x,\bar v).
\]
It is mixed because the underlying first-order mapping is limiting while the normal used to differentiate its graph is regular.

assumptions_latex: \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable on an open set \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(\nabla f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_C^2f(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}\{\lim_k\nabla^2f(x_k):x_k\to\bar x,\ f\text{ twice differentiable at }x_k\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Clarke generalized Hessian for a locally Lipschitz gradient.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 Nonsmooth Analysis I: Clarke's Calculus p. 626
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega_f\) be the full-measure set on which the locally Lipschitz mapping \(\nabla f\) is differentiable. The Clarke generalized Hessian of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
\partial_C^2f(\bar x):=\operatorname{co}\left\{H\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\mid
\exists x_k\in\Omega_f,\ x_k\to\bar x,\ \nabla^2f(x_k)\to H\right\}.
\]
It is a nonempty compact convex set of symmetric matrices. If \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), then \(\partial_C^2f(\bar x)=\{\nabla^2f(\bar x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized Hessian is the convex hull of all limiting classical Hessians at nearby twice-differentiability points.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Generalized Hessians

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Subdifferential of a Finite Smooth Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-index formula for a finite maximum of continuously differentiable functions on an open subset of the ambient space X; the extract does not restrict X to finite dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\subseteq X\) be open and let \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), be continuously differentiable on \(V\). Define \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le n}f_i(x)\) and \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). Then, for every \(x\in V\), \(f\) is regular at \(x\), and \[\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{f_i'(x):i\in I(x)\},\qquad f'(x;v)=\max_{i\in I(x)}\langle f_i'(x),v\rangle\quad\forall v\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum of continuously differentiable functions is regular. Its Clarke subdifferential is the convex hull of the derivatives of the active functions, and its directional derivative is the maximum of their linearized directional values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is regular at }x,\quad\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{co}\{f_i'(x):i\in I(x)\},\quad f'(x;v)=\max_{i\in I(x)}\langle f_i'(x),v\rangle\ \forall v\in X.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise limiting construction with the second variable held fixed in the coderivative input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Regard the partial subgradient mapping as \(\partial_xf:\mathbb{R}^{n+p}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\). Its first-variable partial second-order subdifferential at \(((\bar x,\bar y),\bar v)\) is
\[
\partial_{xx}^2f((\bar x,\bar y),\bar v)(u):=
\{w\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid (w,0)\in D^*(\partial_xf)((\bar x,\bar y),\bar v)(u)\}.
\]
The zero component suppresses dual variation in the second block. More generally, the full coderivative value \(D^*(\partial_xf)((\bar x,\bar y),\bar v)(u)\subset\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p\) records coupled second-order effects in both variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial second-order subdifferential extracts coderivative responses associated with one variable block while suppressing dual variation in the other block.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order directional expansion and solution sensitivity for an SDP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined solution-path stability, second-order value expansion, and characterization of normalized solution increments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widehat x(t)=\widehat x(u_0+td)\) be an optimal solution of \((P_u)\) for \(t\ge0\), with \(\widehat x(t)\to\bar x\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Assume the directional regularity condition (5.231), the strong second-order sufficient conditions (5.232), and \(\mathcal S(PL_d)\ne\varnothing\). Then
\[
\|\widehat x(t)-\bar x\|=O(t),
\]
\[
v(u_0+td)=v(u_0)+t\operatorname{val}(DL_d)+\tfrac12t^2\operatorname{val}(Q_d)+o(t^2),
\]
where
\[
\operatorname{val}(Q_d)=\min_{h\in\mathcal S(PL_d)}\max_{\Omega\in\mathcal S(DL_d)}\left\{D^2L(\bar x,\Omega,u_0)((h,d),(h,d))+\mathcal H(\bar x,\Omega)(h,d)\right\},
\]
\[
D^2L((h,d),(h,d))=h^T\nabla^2_{xx}Lh+2h^T\nabla^2_{xu}Ld+d^T\nabla^2_{uu}Ld,
\]
and, writing \(G=G(\bar x,u_0)\),
\[
\mathcal H(\bar x,\Omega)(h,d)=h^T\mathcal H_{xx}(\Omega)h+2h^T\mathcal H_{xu}(\Omega)d+d^T\mathcal H_{uu}(\Omega)d,
\]
\[
\mathcal H_{xx}=-2G_x^T(\Omega\otimes G^\dagger)G_x,\quad
\mathcal H_{xu}=-2G_x^T(\Omega\otimes G^\dagger)G_u,\quad
\mathcal H_{uu}=-2G_u^T(\Omega\otimes G^\dagger)G_u.
\]
Every accumulation point of \((\widehat x(t)-\bar x)/t\) as \(t\downarrow0\) solves \((Q_d)\). If \((Q_d)\) has the unique solution \(\bar h\), then
\[
\widehat x(t)=\bar x+t\bar h+o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a nonnegative parameter ray, directional regularity, strong second-order sufficiency, and solvability of the linearized primal problem imply Lipschitz stability of the selected SDP solutions. The value admits a second-order expansion whose quadratic coefficient is the value of a primal-dual min-max problem containing Lagrangian Hessian and semidefinite-cone curvature terms. Every limit of the normalized solution increments solves that min-max problem; uniqueness yields a first-order expansion of the solution path.
assumptions_latex: The strong second-order sufficient conditions (5.232) hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\widehat x(t)-\bar x\|=O(t),\quad v(u_0+td)=v(u_0)+t\operatorname{val}(DL_d)+\tfrac12t^2\operatorname{val}(Q_d)+o(t^2);\ \operatorname{Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\widehat x(t)-\bar x}{t}\subseteq\mathcal S(Q_d),\ \text{and uniqueness of }\bar h\in\mathcal S(Q_d)\text{ implies }\widehat x(t)=\bar x+t\bar h+o(t).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiability of a scalar convex subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the equivalent one-sided-derivative characterization and the boundary that nearby subdifferentials need not be single-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb R and x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f). The multifunction \partial f is differentiable at x if \partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\} and there exists D_2f(x)\in\mathbb R such that, for every \varepsilon>0, there is \delta>0 for which |h|\leq\delta and s\in\partial f(x+h) imply |s-Df(x)-D_2f(x)h|\leq\varepsilon|h|. This is equivalent to differentiability at x of either one-sided derivative D_-f or D_+f. It does not require \partial f to be single-valued in a neighborhood of x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex real function at an interior domain point, its subdifferential is differentiable when it is single-valued at that point and every nearby subgradient has the same first-order affine approximation. This is equivalent to differentiability of either one-sided derivative at the point, but does not force nearby subdifferentials to be single-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\},\quad \partial f(x+h)=Df(x)+D_2f(x)h+o(|h|)\ \text{uniformly over its values}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A pointwise and sign-symmetric comparison of the graphical derivative and coderivative of the subgradient mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} and let \bar v\in\partial f(\bar x). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Conditions on the Linearized Equality-Constraint Kernel
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth equality-constrained optimization with \(U_{ad}=U\), using the Lagrangian Hessian in the joint state-control space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\widehat y,\widehat u)\) solve the equality-constrained problem with \(U_{ad}=U\), and let \(\widehat p\) satisfy \(\left(\partial c(\widehat y,\widehat u)/\partial y\right)^*\widehat p=\nabla_yJ(\widehat y,\widehat u)\). Then \(\operatorname{Hess}L(\widehat y,\widehat u,\widehat p)\) is positive semidefinite on \(\ker[\,\partial c/\partial y\ \ \partial c/\partial u\,]\). Conversely, if \((\widehat y,\widehat u,\widehat p)\) satisfies the first-order conditions, the Lagrangian Hessian satisfies the stated Lipschitz condition, and there exists a finite constant \(c\) such that \[(\operatorname{Hess}L(\widehat y,\widehat u,\widehat p)h,h)_{Y\times U}\ge c\,(h,h)_{Y\times U}\] for every \(h\) in that kernel, then \((\widehat y,\widehat u)\) is a local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an equality-constrained optimum, the Lagrangian Hessian is positive semidefinite along directions satisfying the linearized constraints. Conversely, first-order conditions plus the stated coercivity on those directions and Lipschitz continuity of the Lagrangian Hessian imply a local minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(U_{ad}=U\) and \((\widehat y,\widehat u)\) is feasible for the equality-constrained problem.
\(\left(\partial c(\widehat y,\widehat u)/\partial y\right)^*\widehat p=\nabla_yJ(\widehat y,\widehat u)\) for the necessary condition.
Directions \(h=(h_1,h_2)\in Y\times U\) satisfy \([\,\partial c/\partial y\ \ \partial c/\partial u\,]h=0\).
For sufficiency, \((\widehat y,\widehat u,\widehat p)\) satisfies the first-order conditions.
For sufficiency, the Lagrangian Hessian obeys the stated kernel coercivity inequality for a constant \(c<\infty\) and satisfies the Lipschitz condition of the preceding Taylor estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Hess}L(\widehat y,\widehat u,\widehat p)\) is positive semidefinite on the kernel of the linearized constraints at an optimum; under the stated first-order, coercivity, and Lipschitz assumptions, \((\widehat y,\widehat u)\) is a local minimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order subdifferential sum rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three normal and mixed second-order sum-rule regimes in Asplund primal and dual spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varphi_i:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) for \(i=1,2\), let \(\bar y\in\partial(\varphi_1+\varphi_2)(\bar x)\), and suppose \(X\) and \(X^*\) are Asplund. For either \(\partial^2=\partial_N^2\) or \(\partial^2=\partial_M^2\): (i) if \(\varphi_1\in C^1\), \(\bar y_1=\nabla\varphi_1(\bar x)\), \(\bar y_2=\bar y-\bar y_1\), \(\operatorname{gph}\partial\varphi_2\) is locally norm closed, and either \(\varphi_1\in C^{1,1}\) near \(\bar x\) or \(\partial\varphi_2\) is PSNC at \((\bar x,\bar y_2)\) with \(\partial_M^2\varphi_1(\bar x,\bar y_1)(0)\cap[-\partial_M^2\varphi_2(\bar x,\bar y_2)(0)]=\{0\}\), then for every \(u\in X^{**}\), \(\partial^2(\varphi_1+\varphi_2)(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\subset\partial^2\varphi_1(\bar x,\bar y_1)(u)+\partial^2\varphi_2(\bar x,\bar y_2)(u)\). (ii) The same inclusion holds for a fixed decomposition \((\bar y_1,\bar y_2)\) when both functions are locally l.s.c.; the decomposition mapping \(S(x,y)=\{(y_1,y_2):y_i\in\partial\varphi_i(x),\ y_1+y_2=y\}\) is inner semicontinuous there; both subdifferential graphs are locally norm closed; one subdifferential is PSNC; the preceding second-order qualification holds; and, on a neighborhood \(U\), \(\partial^\infty\varphi_1(x)\cap[-\partial^\infty\varphi_2(x)]=\{0\}\), one function is SNEC at every \(x\in U\), and both functions are lower regular there. The singular qualification and SNEC assumptions are automatic if one summand is locally Lipschitz. (iii) If \(S\) is inner semicompact at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), the subdifferential graphs are norm closed near \(\bar x\), and the assumptions of (ii) hold for every decomposition in \(S(\bar x,\bar y)\), then the left-hand side is contained in the union, over all such decompositions, of the corresponding sums of second-order subdifferentials.

A fixed-decomposition rule follows under local graph closedness and suitable PSNC, second-order, singular-subdifferential, SNEC, lower-regularity, and inner-semicontinuity conditions. With inner semicompactness and these conditions for every multiplier decomposition, the result becomes a union over all decompositions. Local Lipschitz continuity of one summand makes the singular qualification and SNEC requirements automatic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian Operator on a Real Hilbert Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical twice-differentiable real-valued functions on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable at \(u\), with symmetric bilinear second derivative \(D^2f(u)\). For each \(h_1\in U\), let \(v(h_1)\in U\) be the Riesz representative satisfying \(D^2f(u)[h_1,h_2]=(v(h_1),h_2)\) for every \(h_2\in U\). The Hessian operator is \(\operatorname{Hess}f(u):U\to U\), \(\operatorname{Hess}f(u)h_1=v(h_1)\); it is linear and self-adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hessian operator maps each direction to the Riesz representative of the second derivative with its first argument fixed. Because the second derivative is symmetric bilinear, this operator is linear and self-adjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^2f(u)[h_1,h_2]=(\operatorname{Hess}f(u)h_1,h_2)\) for all \(h_1,h_2\in U\), and \(\operatorname{Hess}f(u)\) is linear and self-adjoint.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz stability of GVIs with composite fields
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two Banach-space regimes giving second-order sufficient conditions, a conditional necessity result, and quantitative Lipschitz estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be defined by (4.67), with \(g:X\times Y\to W\), \(\varphi:W\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(f:X\times Y\to W^*\), \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}S\), \(\bar w=g(\bar x,\bar y)\), and \(\bar q=-f(\bar x,\bar y)\). (i) Suppose \(X,Y\) are Asplund, \(W\) is Banach, \(g=g(y)\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar y\) with surjective \(\nabla g(\bar y)\), and \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with surjective \(\nabla_xf(\bar x,\bar y)\). Then
\[0\in\nabla_yf(\bar x,\bar y)^*u+\nabla g(\bar y)^*\partial_N^2\varphi(\bar w,\bar q)(u)\ \Longrightarrow\ u=0\]
is sufficient for the Lipschitz-like property of \(S\); it is necessary if \(S\) is strongly coderivatively normal there, in particular if \(\dim Y<\infty\). If also \(\dim X<\infty\) and \(\partial\varphi\) is SNC at \((\bar w,\bar q)\), then
\[\operatorname{lip}S(\bar x,\bar y)=\sup\{\|\nabla_xf(\bar x,\bar y)^*u\|:\exists z^*\in\partial_N^2\varphi(\bar w,\bar q)(u),\ \|\nabla_yf(\bar x,\bar y)^*u+\nabla g(\bar y)^*z^*\|\le1\}.\]
(ii) Suppose \(X,Y,W,W^*\) are Asplund, \(g\) is continuous and \(f\) strictly Lipschitz at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), \(\operatorname{gph}\partial\varphi\) is norm-closed around \((\bar w,\bar q)\), and (4.72) holds. If
\[(x^*,0)\in\partial\langle u,f\rangle(\bar x,\bar y)+D_N^*g(\bar x,\bar y)\circ\partial_N^2\varphi(\bar w,\bar q)(u)\ \Longrightarrow\ x^*=u=0,\]
and either \(g\) is PSNC while \(\partial\varphi\) is SNC, or \(g\) is SNC while \(\partial\varphi^{-1}\) is PSNC, at the stated reference points, then \(S\) is Lipschitz-like. If additionally \(\dim X<\infty\),
\[\operatorname{lip}S(\bar x,\bar y)\le\sup\{\|x^*\|:\exists u\in W^{**},\ (x^*,-y^*)\in\partial\langle u,f\rangle(\bar x,\bar y)+D_N^*g(\bar x,\bar y)\circ\partial_N^2\varphi(\bar w,\bar q)(u),\ \|y^*\|\le1\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For composite-field GVIs, second-order subdifferential nondegeneracy conditions yield Lipschitz-like stability. Under strong coderivative normality the smooth-regime condition is also necessary, and finite-dimensional parameter spaces admit the stated exact or upper modulus formulas.
assumptions_latex: \bar w=g(\bar x,\bar y),\quad \bar q=-f(\bar x,\bar y)
\text{The alternative assumptions of cases (i) or (ii) hold}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The applicable second-order implication ensures that }S\text{ is Lipschitz-like, with the stated necessity and modulus conclusions under the additional hypotheses.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proto-derivative and Aubin criterion for parameterized variational conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of the solution mapping for a smooth perturbation of a fully amenable subgradient inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), let \(F:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be \(C^1\), and define
\[
S(w,u)=\{x\mid u\in F(w,x)+\partial f(x)\}.
\]
If \(\bar x\in S(\bar w,\bar u)\) and \(f\) is fully amenable at \(\bar x\), set \(\bar v=\bar u-F(\bar w,\bar x)\),
\[
\Phi(w',x')=\nabla_wF(\bar w,\bar x)w'+\nabla_xF(\bar w,\bar x)x',\qquad
\varphi(x')=\tfrac12 d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(x').
\]
Then \(S\) is proto-differentiable at \((\bar w,\bar u)\) for \(\bar x\), with
\[
DS(\bar w,\bar u\mid\bar x)(w',u')=\{x'\mid u'\in\Phi(w',x')+\partial\varphi(x')\}.
\]
Furthermore, \(S\) is graphically Lipschitzian of dimension \(d+2n\) locally and has the Aubin property at \((\bar w,\bar u)\) for \(\bar x\) if and only if
\[
-\nabla_xF(\bar w,\bar x)^*z\in D^*(\partial f)(\bar x\mid\bar v)(z)\Longrightarrow z=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth parameterized perturbation of the subdifferential of a fully amenable function, the solution mapping is proto-differentiable. Its proto-derivative is the solution set of the linearized smooth term plus the subdifferential of half the second epi-derivative. The solution mapping is locally graphically Lipschitzian, and it has the Aubin property exactly when the displayed adjoint-coderivative implication has only the zero solution.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is fully amenable at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is proto-differentiable with the stated linearized second-epi-derivative formula; it is locally graphically Lipschitzian and has the Aubin property}\iff[-\nabla_xF(\bar w,\bar x)^*z\in D^*(\partial f)(\bar x\mid\bar v)(z)\Rightarrow z=0].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proto-derivative and Aubin criterion for a perturbed subgradient system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order sensitivity of a parameterized subgradient optimality mapping under prox-regularity and subdifferential continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
S(u,v)=\{(x,y)\mid (v,y)\in\partial f(x,u)\},\qquad (\bar x,\bar y)\in S(\bar u,\bar v),
\]
where \(f:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at \((\bar x,\bar u)\) for \((\bar v,\bar y)\). Then \(S\) is proto-differentiable at \((\bar u,\bar v)\) for \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(f\) is twice epi-differentiable there for \((\bar v,\bar y)\). In that case, with \(h=\tfrac12 d^2f(\bar x,\bar u\mid\bar v,\bar y)\),
\[
DS(\bar u,\bar v\mid\bar x,\bar y)(u',v')=\{(x',y')\mid(v',y')\in\partial h(x',u')\}.
\]
Moreover, \(S\) is graphically Lipschitzian of dimension \(m+n\) locally, and it has the Aubin property at \((\bar u,\bar v)\) for \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if
\[
(0,y')\in D^*(\partial f)((\bar x,\bar u)\mid(\bar v,\bar y))(x',0)\Longrightarrow (x',y')=(0,0).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a prox-regular, subdifferentially continuous parameterized function, the associated subgradient optimality mapping is proto-differentiable exactly when the function is twice epi-differentiable. Its proto-derivative is the subgradient system generated by half the second epi-derivative. The mapping is locally graphically Lipschitzian, and its Aubin property is equivalent to the stated coderivative kernel condition.

f\text{ is subdifferentially continuous at }(\bar x,\bar u)\text{ for }(\bar v,\bar y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is proto-differentiable}\iff f\text{ is twice epi-differentiable},\quad DS\text{ has the stated second-epi-derivative representation, and }S\text{ has the Aubin property}\iff\ker D^*(\partial f)\text{ satisfies the stated triviality condition}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Upper Limit and Exposed-Face Localization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded boundary-direction result for closed proper convex functions; the iterated directional notation is retained from the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be closed, proper, and convex, let x\in\operatorname{dom}f, and let x_i\in\operatorname{dom}f\setminus\{x\} satisfy x_i\to x and (x_i-x)/\|x_i-x\|\to y. Assume f'(x;y)>-\infty and that \{x+\lambda y:\lambda\ge0\} meets \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f). Then, for every z\in\mathbb{R}^n, \limsup_{i\to\infty}f'(x_i;z)\le f'(x;y;z). Moreover, for every \varepsilon>0 there exists i_0 such that \partial f(x_i)\subseteq\partial f(x)_y+\varepsilon B for all i\ge i_0, where \partial f(x)_y=\{x^*\in\partial f(x):y\in N_{\partial f(x)}(x^*)\} and B is the Euclidean unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When domain points approach a point along a limiting direction whose forward ray reaches the domain interior, directional derivatives at the approaching points have an upper limit controlled by the corresponding iterated directional derivative. Nearby subgradients eventually concentrate near the face of the limiting subdifferential at which the approach direction is normal.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall z\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ \limsup_{i\to\infty}f'(x_i;z)\le f'(x;y;z),\qquad \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists i_0\ \forall i\ge i_0:\ \partial f(x_i)\subseteq\partial f(x)_y+\varepsilon B.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cubic Remainder Estimate for a Lipschitz Hessian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A second-order expansion estimate on an open convex subset of a Hilbert space, preserving the expression stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space, let \(U\subset H\) be open and convex, and let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable. If \(\|\operatorname{Hess}f(u)-\operatorname{Hess}f(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|\) for all \(u,v\in U\), where \(L<\infty\), then for all \(u,v\in U\), \[\left|f(u)-f(v)+(\nabla f(u),v-u)+\frac12(\operatorname{Hess}f(u)(v-u),v-u)\right|\le\frac{L}{6}\|u-v\|^3.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open convex subset of a Hilbert space, the stated second-order expression has absolute value at most L/6 times the cube of the distance whenever the Hessian is L-Lipschitz.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-C2 Characterization via Prox-Regularity and Strict Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence and local differentiable specialization on an open set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $O\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be open. If $f$ is lower-$\mathcal C^2$ on $O$, then $f$ is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at every point of $O$ and is strictly continuous on $O$. Conversely, if $f$ is prox-regular and strictly continuous on $O$, then $f$ is lower-$\mathcal C^2$ on $O$. In particular, if $f$ is prox-regular at $\bar x$ and strictly differentiable there, then $f$ is lower-$\mathcal C^2$ on a neighborhood of $\bar x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open set, lower-C2 functions are everywhere prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous and are strictly continuous. Conversely, prox-regularity together with strict continuity characterizes lower-C2 functions. At a point of strict differentiability, prox-regularity therefore implies a local lower-C2 representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ lower-}\mathcal C^2\text{ on }O\Rightarrow f\text{ prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous pointwise and strictly continuous on }O;\quad f\text{ prox-regular and strictly continuous on }O\Rightarrow f\text{ lower-}\mathcal C^2\text{ on }O.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Prox-Regularity of a Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise prox-regularity relative to a specified limiting subgradient, and its all-subgradients variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is prox-regular at $\bar x$ for $\bar v$ if $f$ is finite and locally lower semicontinuous at $\bar x$, $\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)$, and there exist $\varepsilon>0$ and $\rho\geq0$ such that
\[
f(x')\geq f(x)+\langle v,x'-x\rangle-\frac{\rho}{2}\lVert x'-x\rVert^2
\]
for every $x'\in\mathbb B(\bar x,\varepsilon)$ whenever $v\in\partial f(x)$, $\lVert v-\bar v\rVert<\varepsilon$, $\lVert x-\bar x\rVert<\varepsilon$, and $f(x)<f(\bar x)+\varepsilon$. It is prox-regular at $\bar x$ if this holds for every $\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is prox-regular at x-bar for a subgradient v-bar when it is finite and locally lower semicontinuous there and admits a uniform local quadratic lower support inequality for all nearby graph points of its subdifferential satisfying the stated value bound. It is prox-regular at x-bar when this holds for every subgradient at x-bar.
assumptions_latex: f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\text{ and }f\text{ is locally lsc at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\varepsilon>0,\ \rho\geq0\ \text{such that the stated quadratic support inequality holds under all specified locality and value conditions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization of Functions with Strictly Continuous Gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence on an open set and its prox-regularity consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $O\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be open. A function $f$ is of class $\mathcal C^{1+}$ on $O$, meaning that it is differentiable and $\nabla f$ is strictly continuous, if and only if $f$ is both lower-$\mathcal C^2$ and upper-$\mathcal C^2$ on $O$. Consequently, every such $f$ is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at every point of $O$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an open set, differentiability with a strictly continuous gradient is equivalent to being simultaneously lower-C2 and upper-C2. Every function in this class is consequently prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous throughout the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\mathcal C^{1+}(O)\iff f\text{ is lower-}\mathcal C^2\text{ and upper-}\mathcal C^2\text{ on }O,\qquad f\in\mathcal C^{1+}(O)\Rightarrow f\text{ is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous on }O.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is subdifferentially continuous at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if every sequence \((x_k,v_k)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) satisfying
\[
(x_k,v_k)\to(\bar x,\bar v)
\]
also satisfies
\[
f(x_k)\to f(\bar x).
\]
Equivalently, the value mapping \((x,v)\mapsto f(x)\), restricted to \(\operatorname{gph}\partial f\), is continuous at \((\bar x,\bar v)\). Subdifferential continuity at \(\bar x\) means that this condition holds for every \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearby graph points of the subgradient mapping must carry function values converging to the reference value.
